claims.claim: Data were acquired at 100 kHz for voltage-clamp experiments.

claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methods for data acquisition.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the biological context and theoretical framework for homeostatic plasticity. Claims describe that neural systems use homeostatic plasticity to maintain function (C1), that such mechanisms have mainly been demonstrated under artificial/pathological conditions (C2), and that bullfrogs provide a natural model where respiratory circuits remain inactive for months during winter (C3). The theoretical basis for synaptic scaling and compensatory mechanisms is established through general principles (C8, C9, C33, C41) and literature review (C10).
results.evaluation: These claims establish well-supported background knowledge and rationale for the study. The claims about homeostatic plasticity mechanisms (C1, C8, C9, C33, C41) are supported by established neuroscience literature. The gap in knowledge (C2, C10) and the biological model (C3) are appropriately cited and provide clear justification for the experimental approach.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior work demonstrating homeostatic plasticity in various systems and establishes the biological characteristics of bullfrog overwintering. Examples include synaptic scaling in rodent visual cortex (C11), compensatory mechanisms in Xenopus (C12), and plasticity in crustacean circuits (C13). Bullfrog-specific biology is described: overwintering without lung breathing (C14), maintained locomotor capacity (C15), respiratory muscle inactivity during cold submergence (C16), and immediate recovery of breathing function upon warming (C17-C20). Prior work showing increases in excitatory transmission during inactivity is cited (C21, C22).
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately cite and summarize prior literature to establish context. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made, establishing both general principles of homeostatic plasticity across systems and specific characteristics of the bullfrog model. The claims are properly attributed to cited sources.

results.result: Winter inactivity increases mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer in respiratory motoneurons without changing frequency. Claims report that mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer increased after overwintering (C23, C81, C82), while frequency did not change (C24, C83), suggesting similar numbers of glutamate release sites (C25). Input resistance and rise time were unchanged (C28, C29), and all mEPSCs were blocked by DNQX (C80), indicating the changes reflect enhanced postsynaptic AMPA receptor function rather than dendritic filtering changes (C27, C30). Charge transfer is noted as more robust against space clamp errors (C26).
results.evaluation: These claims are well-supported by the experimental data in Figure 2. The statistical analyses show significant increases in amplitude (p=0.0073) and charge transfer (p=0.0017) with no change in frequency (p=0.8227). The interpretation that changes reflect postsynaptic AMPA receptor enhancement is reasonable given unchanged input resistance and rise time, and is supported by appropriate citation (Han and Stevens, 2009). Sample sizes (n=16 per group) are adequate.

results.result: The increase in synaptic strength follows multiplicative synaptic scaling. Claims establish that synaptic scaling typically follows a multiplicative relationship in culture (C31) and in vivo (C32), while LTP follows an exponential relationship (C34). The rank-order plot of mEPSCs fits a linear regression well (r²=0.99, C35) but not an exponential curve (r²=0.73, C36), with a slope of 1.51 (C37, C38). When the winter inactivity distribution is divided by this scaling factor, it overlaps the control distribution (C39, C67, C85), while the unscaled distributions differ significantly (C84). This indicates slow, global scaling rather than rapid LTP-like mechanisms (C68).
results.evaluation: The scaling analysis in Figure 3 provides strong evidence for multiplicative synaptic scaling. The linear fit (r²=0.99) is substantially better than the exponential fit (r²=0.73), and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test shows the scaled distribution overlaps controls (p=0.1403) while unscaled distributions differ (p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶). The methodology follows established approaches (Turrigiano et al., 1998; Gainey et al., 2009) and the interpretation is appropriate. The exclusion of scaled values below detection threshold (C121) is properly justified.

results.result: Respiratory motoneurons do not show enhanced intrinsic excitability after winter inactivity. While compensatory changes in intrinsic currents typically manifest as enhanced excitability (C42), firing frequency did not differ between groups at any current level (C43), F-I gain was unchanged (C44, C86, p=0.9147), and resting membrane potential was similar (C45, p=0.8269). These results suggest motoneurons do not enhance excitability in response to winter inactivity (C46).
results.evaluation: The current clamp data in Figure 4 clearly show no differences in excitability between control and winter inactivity motoneurons. The ANCOVA analysis appropriately tests for differences in F-I relationships, and the lack of significant differences is well-documented. This negative result is important as it indicates the compensatory response is specific to synaptic rather than intrinsic properties. Sample sizes are adequate (n=16 per group).

results.result: Up-scaling of AMPA receptors enhances the contribution of AMPA receptors to respiratory motor output after winter inactivity. Claims establish that respiratory CPG activity is transmitted via glutamatergic synapses (C47, C48) and that motor amplitude reflects synaptic properties while frequency reflects rhythm generation (C49, C50). Prior work showed low DNQX concentrations don't affect amplitude in controls (C51, C52). The current data confirm this in control frogs (C53) but show that winter inactivity frogs exhibit ~40% reduction in CN X burst amplitude and area with DNQX (C54, C61, C70, C87, C88), indicating increased reliance on AMPA receptors (C55, C59, C69). Both groups showed similar ~80% reduction in frequency (C57, C89), suggesting rhythm generator AMPA sensitivity was unchanged (C58). Winter inactivity frogs had higher baseline frequency (C56, C90).
results.evaluation: The extracellular recording data in Figure 5 provide strong functional evidence that synaptic scaling preserves motor output. The differential effect of DNQX on amplitude (significant reduction in winter inactivity but not controls, p=0.0286) while frequency responses are similar (both ~80% reduction) supports the interpretation that scaling specifically affects motoneuron transmission rather than rhythm generation. The recovery toward baseline after washout (Figure 5—supplement 1) supports reversibility. Sample size (n=4 per group) is modest but consistent with similar studies and the effect sizes are large.

results.result: Synaptic scaling of AMPA receptors on respiratory motoneurons preserves respiratory motor output and contributes to normal ventilation after months of inactivity. The main conclusion (C7, C73) integrates findings that up-scaling is physiologically relevant (C60), that motor amplitude corresponds with muscle drive (C62, C72), that ventilation is normal after winter inactivity in intact frogs (C63), and that motor output would be reduced without scaling (C71). The authors conclude scaling contributes to normal ventilation after prolonged inactivity (C64).
results.evaluation: This conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from cellular (increased mEPSC amplitude/charge transfer), systems (multiplicative scaling), and functional (DNQX sensitivity of motor output) levels. The logic connecting cellular changes to behavioral function is sound, though the link to intact animal ventilation (C63, C64) is inferential since ventilation was not directly measured in this study. The claim is appropriately qualified as 'may contribute' (C64). The interpretation that output would be smaller without scaling (C71) is directly supported by the DNQX experiments.

results.result: AMPA receptor upregulation does not underlie increased fictive breathing frequency after winter inactivity, suggesting distinct compensatory mechanisms regulate frequency versus amplitude. The elevated baseline frequency in winter inactivity preparations (C74) likely involves different mechanisms than AMPA receptor scaling, implying rhythm generating circuits use distinct compensation mechanisms (C75).
results.evaluation: This interpretation is supported by the observation that both groups show similar proportional reductions in frequency with DNQX (~80%) despite winter inactivity frogs having higher baseline frequency. This dissociation between amplitude effects (differential DNQX sensitivity) and frequency effects (similar DNQX sensitivity) reasonably suggests distinct mechanisms. However, the specific mechanisms for frequency enhancement remain speculative and are appropriately identified as unknown.

results.result: Anatomical and methodological claims establish that the recorded neurons are laryngeal motoneurons innervating the glottal dilator muscle. The glottal dilator gates airflow during ventilation (C76) and is innervated by the laryngeal branch of vagus nerve from the fourth rootlet (C77, C78). Laryngeal motoneurons are morphologically distinct with larger soma diameters (C79). Methods describe selecting slices within 600 μm of obex (C102) and neurons with soma >20 μm (C103), and that 3 hours was sufficient for retrograde labeling (C100). SN II and CN X activity corresponds with respiratory CPG activity (C113, C114).
results.evaluation: The anatomical claims are well-supported by appropriate citations (Gans et al., 1969; Stuesse et al., 1984; Matesz and Székely, 1996; etc.). The methodological approach for identifying the correct motoneuron population is sound and based on established anatomical knowledge. The retrograde labeling is demonstrated in Figure 1. The criteria for neuron selection are clearly justified by the cited anatomical literature.

results.result: Detailed methodological claims describe experimental procedures, data acquisition, analysis methods, and statistical approaches. These include animal care approval (C94), experimental groups and conditions (C95-C98), tissue preparation (C99, C101), recording parameters (C104-C107), inclusion/exclusion criteria (C108-C110), pharmacological protocols (C111, C112, C117), recording methods (C115, C116), data analysis procedures (C118-C129), sample size justification (C130, C131), and statistical threshold (C132).
results.evaluation: The methods are described in appropriate detail and follow standard practices for patch-clamp electrophysiology and extracellular recordings. Key parameters are specified (holding potentials, filter settings, sampling rates, drug concentrations, etc.). Quality control measures are described (series resistance monitoring, membrane potential criteria). The data analysis methods are clearly explained and appropriate. Sample sizes are justified by comparison to similar studies. The statistical approaches are standard and appropriate for the data types.
